rv.q: And though the play fixes on physics, rest assured the chemistry is ample.
Constellations is the first Broadway opening of the year and it sets the bar high.
You are probably more apt to discover your own self in the characters of “Constellations,” which was first staged in London in 2012 and arrives here in a Manhattan Theater Club production.
Her style as the brilliant, desperately needy Marianne is mercurial — and enchanting.
Wilson and Gyllenhaal place it in a universe where Broadway vehicles have heart.
Constellations is smart but not dry; its focus is on the personal and emotional.
But it does get wearing, even at just 70 minutes.

More than anything else, "Constellations" is a touching love story, a deeply universal one - or should I say, multiversal?

Jake Gyllenhaal and 'The Affair's' Golden Globe winner Ruth Wilson ace their Broadway debuts in 'Constellations,' a compact play with big ideas about life, love and death that is, happily, as brainy as it is sweet-hearted...
If 'Constellations' begins as something of an amusing theatrical stunt, it evolves into something much more powerful.

The only real drawback to this kind of story-telling is that it’s something of an effort to ever really attach to Marianne or Roland because, by design, they have so many darn personalities.

The play manages to feel slight and jam-packed at the same time, combining an uninteresting boy-meets-girl romance and a well-worn premise of right turn versus left turn with a hard-to-follow structure.

cn.t: Critics praise this inventive quantum physics romance for its emotional depth and the stellar chemistry between Gyllenhaal and Wilson, though some find the multiverse concept more gimmicky than profound. Most agree it's both brainy and unexpectedly moving.
